content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper aims to improve Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH). The paper shows that the combination of several techniques, such as different activations, skip connection, and knowledge distillation, can improve the performance of the sparse sub-network obtained from dense networks. The paper validates the method on some networks such as ResNet and MobileNet. Most experiments shown in the paper are conducted on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100.
content.main_review:
### Strengths
1. The proposed methods in the paper can help improve the performance of the sparse networks obtained using LTH.
2. The proposed methods are well ablated.
3. The paper shows various experiments on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 to validate the methods.

### Weaknesses
1. The paper claims that LTH is one of the most effective methods of deploying computationally expensive models on devices. However, the paper didn't show any benefits when deploying the proposed model on devices. Some techniques introduced in the paper, such as additional skip connection, can increase the latency of the model. 
2. The technical novelty of the paper is rather limited. The paper seems didn't propose new techniques; instead, it combines different tricks, such as different activations, skip connection, and knowledge distillation, to improve the classification accuracy.
3. Some techniques used in the paper, such as changing activation or adding skip connection, actually change the architecture of the sparse network. It's not a fair comparison with other LHT methods. I guess using more aggressive network changing methods such as network architecture searching could even improve the performance.
4. The experiments are not extensive, considering the paper is more like empirical work. Most experiments in the paper are conducted on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100, which are very small datasets. The author claims experiments on Tiny-ImageNet, but there is only one experiment on Tiny-ImageNet (Figure 7), and the architecture used is not clarified in the paper. 
5. I would suggest the authors have more experiments on ImageNet. Besides the networks used in the paper, I would suggest having deeper and more challenging networks, such as ResNet 50 and MobileNet V2.
content.summary_of_the_review: While the proposed methods can achieve better results than existing LHT methods, the novelty is rather limited. The paper is more like an empirical report with a combination of different training tricks. Also, the experiments on limited network architectures and small datasets are not convincing. Therefore, I lean towards rejection.

content.title: Author Response to vJA7
content.comment:
With our respects for your time and efforts, unfortunately, it appears to us that you were not understanding or interpreting our results in the correct context. We politely hope our clarifications below will clear most, if not all, of your questions

We identify the LTH sparse re-training goal and troubleshoot its overlooked problems (which is novel); and then refer to simple tools to solving those problems (we could have been “novel”, but we purposely avoid so since we believe no reinventing wheels is the right thing to do for science, if well-defined techniques can do the job right - “Simplicity is the final achievement. ”, well-said by Chopin). In other words, what makes this paper truly novel is knowing “where should be fixed”, besides (and more than) “how to concretely fix”. 

1) **Challenging prolonged LTH belief** that sparse ticket retraining should stick to the protocol of dense network training and sparse mask finding. We would like to clarify that **LTH is a three-step process: 1) Train the dense network 2) Iterative pruning to find the sparse mask 3) Retrain the identified pruned mask in isolation to full accuracy.**
Most if not all existing well-established LTH literature use the same architecture blocks, initialization techniques, and training recipe used by dense networks in step 1.  However, it is not clear if blindly inheriting dense network protocols is optimal for sparse networks. We are first to raise a direct question on inheritance, and experimentally shown that making sparse re-training purposely misaligned in some way from dense training (step 3) can make the found sparse subnetwork work even better. We want to highlight that we are only making changes in the step 3 of LTH and completely independent of either dense training or identifying prune masks. This novelty has been also acknowledged by *Reviewer eSrF (‘inspiring challenger to many “commonsense” in LTH’)*

2) We are **first to identify a set of simple and well-defined techniques which can help sparse retraining step of LTH** to match the equivalent performance of the common practice of weight rewinding [1], which have many drawbacks (struggle to find rewind point, bookkeeping the weights of dense network during their training, entwine of rewind point to model architecture, etc) which has been appreciated by *Reviewer puN9 (‘compelling results for high sparsity as compared to LTH rewinding’)*. Even though these techniques have been known in the dense network training regime, they have been hidden/unexplored in sparse retraining step for LTH because of the clouded wisdom that sparse retraining need to stick to protocols of dense network training. *Reviewer eSrF acknowledges this as “established the improved sparse re-training step as a hidden gem”*.


**[Cons1: Unjustified claim of LTH being best]** It is unfortunate that you seem to severely misunderstand our work’s context, which all other three reviewers seem to get correctly. 

This paper is NOT at all a practical mobile-model-deployment paper (even the authors are actually experts here too, and familiar with the effect of residual skip-connections, eg. RepVGG[1]). Instead, LTH  is a scientific topic on probing the trainability of sparse NNs (how to train subnetworks identified by LTH more effectively to achieve significantly better performance). We clarify that we have never made such a claim that *“LTH is one of the most effective methods of deploying computationally expensive models on devices”* as you accused. 

We state that most existing models are overparameterized. Towards fixing the (potentially unnecessary) overparameterization, a significant amount of work is currently going on, and LTH is one of the many approaches with the benefit that the pruned subnetworks identified from LTH can be trained in isolation from scratch. Its practical usage has been also discovered in parameter- or resource-efficient transfer learning, although that is out of our scope here. So, we sincerely suggest that your weakness point 1 has no relevance here.

**[Cons2: Insufficient Experiments]** We would like to highlight that we have conducted extensive experiments to show performance margins generalization across datasets (CIFAR10, CIFAR100, TinyImageNet) and architectures (Vgg16, ResNet-18/ResNet-34, MobileNet). **Reviewers eSrF** have appreciated our effort *“Experiments are thorough and strong”*. We are thankful for pointing out that our TinyImageNet experiment doesn’t mention the architecture used in the experiment (ResNet-18) and we will correct it in the current revision. As suggested we will add additional experiments related to ResNet50 and TinyImageNet as soon as possible.

content.title: Author Response to vJA7
content.comment:
**[Cons3: Our architecture tweaking methods are not comparable]** We completely and strongly disagree with your comment - this falls out of the LTH context again. 

Let us clarify that our architecture tweaks are Plug-n-Play techniques which can be easily adapted to sparse subnetworks identified during the LTH sparse subnetwork finding step (step 2). We show that by incorporating these techniques, we can effectively improve the sparse subnetwork performance. 

More aggressive NAS is a different approach that has nothing to do with what we are looking into here (improving sparse network trainability) -- we cannot understand how this jumps into the question. NAS is way more expensive and case-specific compared to the generally applicable, light-weight tweaks that we proposed here. The authors, being NAS experts too, are also unaware of any NAS method direction searching on the elementwise sparsity level. 

All other reviewers have identified the no issue with comparability of our techniques and they have acknowledged (eSrF, puN9, and NPsy) the compelling performance of our methods.

We hope our responses have clarified many of your concerns, and please do not hesitate to let us know what else we could do in order to convince you for a rating upgrade.

[1] Ding, Xiaohan, et al. "Repvgg: Making vgg-style convnets great again." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2021

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors propose several "tweaks" to sparse re-training of lottery tickets that have been identified by iterative magnitude pruning (IMP). These tweaks include 
1) the replacement of ReLU activation functions by smooth activation functions,
2) the use of soft-labels instead of one-hot labels, 
3) learned layer-wise rescaling of the initial parameters to enable effective gradient steps initially, 
4) the injection of new skip connections to avoid layer collapse. 
The tweaks are compared and combined with weight rewinding.
Experiments on CIFAR10, CIRAR100, any TinyImageNet suggest a superior performance of the tweaks over vanilla IMP.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
+ IMP with the proposed tweaks seems to outperform the vanilla IMP across architectures and studied datasets.
+ The authors also tried training with a teacher network.
+ The change of loss surface with regard to the tweaks is analysed indicating that flatter minima are identified with the help of the tweaks.

Weaknesses:
- No error bars are reported. In consideration that pruning results are subject to high levels of noise, this makes it impossible to assess whether the gains over LTH are significant.
- None of the proposed tweaks is novel but is a standard approach used in deep learning.
- All experiments are limited to image classification problems and none of the datasets is really large scale (like ImageNet). For a purely experimental paper that claims to achieve new state-of-the-art results, this experimental evidence seems a bit weak. It is thus unclear whether the proposed tweaks are useful in different settings and tasks. 
- Only comparisons with vanilla LTH are presented. However, a multitude of other techniques have been proposed to address shortcomings of IMP (see e.g. synflow [7] to prevent layer collapse or [1,3]). The claim that the authors achieve a new state of the art is thus not really justified.
- It is unclear what the specific role of the single tweaks is and whether they are actually superior to similar proposals in the literature.
a) For instance, is it really the smoothing affect that helps when replacing ReLUs by smoother activation functions after pruning? Maybe similar results could be achieved by training from the start with smoother activation functions? Also the impact of this tweak does not seem to be consistently positive.
(The authors are not the first to try out activation functions that are different from ReLUs in the context of the LTH.)
b) Skip-connections: A couple of architectures naturally have skip-connections. Are this skip-connections helpful in this context? 
I would expect a deeper analysis of what their specific role is and what happens to them during pruning. E.g.: Are these skip connections actually pruned away or preserved? 
The experimental results indicate that additional skip connections can also harm the performance of relatively dense networks.
Do the authors suggest that skip connections should only be added after aggressive pruning?
If skip connections are beneficial: Do additional skip connections actually prevent layer collapse and are all other parameters removed from a skipped layer? (Is the layer thus effectively removed?) 
Yet, skip connections can have multiple benefits also in training deep dense neural networks, which leaves the questions: How have the blocks with skip connections been initialised? Do these parameter initialisations respect different layer densities and different pruning stages?
In dense training, skip connections can be quite helpful and stabilise training if used in the right way. 
c) Re-scaling of initial parameters: Is the proposed learned re-scaling more effective than orthogonal repair [1]? Does it add value in comparison with [2], which does not even require learning of the scaling factors? 
- Technically, the claim that the authors are the first to explore LTH sparse re-training under different conditions than dense training seems to be an overstatement. All pruning at initialisation methods do that. [2] specifically addresses the parameter initialisation. [4] makes several proposals, e.g., adapting the Drop-Out rate. Adding also links instead of only removing links is also not such an unusual idea. See, e.g., [6]. The authors really have to show that their proposal works better than others.

Points of minor critique and open questions:
- The visualisation of the loss landscape is not explained at all. What are the axes?
- A couple of details are missing on how exactly the tweaks are performed. For instance, how are the layers re-scaled? How are the scaling factors trained? How many skip-connections are added? Which smoothing parameter is used for the soft-labels?
- All of the tweaks introduce additional hyper-parameters that have to be tuned in case of different applications.
- The authors did not test whether they find actually meaningful lottery ticket architectures (see [5]).

Literature:
[1] A Signal Propagation Perspective for Pruning Neural Networks at Initialization, ICLR 2020.
[2] Robust Pruning at Initialization, ICLR 2021.
[3] Winning the Lottery with Continuous Sparsification, NeurIPS 2020.
[4] Learning both Weights and Connections for Efficient Neural Networks, NIPS 2015.
[5] Sanity-Checking Pruning Methods: Random Tickets can Win the Jackpot, NeurIPS 2020.
[6] Sparse Training via Boosting Pruning Plasticity with Neuroregeneration, NeurIPS 2021.
[7] Pruning neural networks without any data by iteratively conserving synaptic flow, NeurIPS 2020.
----------------------------------------------------------
Post-rebuttal update:
----------------------------------------------------------
As the authors have presented additional experiments and compared their approach with multiple other methods, I am convinced that their tweaks can improve sparse training.
I have raised my score to 6 accordingly. However, I reserve doubts that the paper is interesting enough for acceptance at ICLR, since it does not present novel ideas in the context of deep learning. Furthermore, the details of the approach are still not well understandable (see my my points of minor critique which have not been addressed in the updated draft).
content.summary_of_the_review: A multitude of techniques are presented to improve Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) to identify lottery tickets. The presented experiments are encouraging that vanilla IMP can be outperformed but the proposed tweaks are neither particularly novel nor are they compared with similar ideas in the literature or their impact on sparse training thoroughly analysed. Therefore, I believe that the work is not ready for publication at ICLR in this form.

content.title: Author Response to NPsy
content.comment:
Many thanks for reviewing our paper. We provide pointwise responses to your concerns.

**[Cons1: Novelty Concerns ?]** We respectfully disagree - we identify the LTH sparse re-training goal and troubleshoot its overlooked problems (which is novel); and then refer to simple tools to solving those problems (we could have been “novel”, but we purposely avoid so since we believe no reinventing wheels is the right thing to do for science, if well-defined techniques can do the job right - “Simplicity is the final achievement. ”, well-said by Chopin). In other words, what makes this paper truly novel is knowing “where should be fixed”, besides (and more than) “how to concretely fix”. 

Our paper’s novelty mainly lies in the following two aspects:

1) **Challenging prolonged LTH belief** that sparse ticket retraining should stick to the protocol of dense network training and sparse mask finding. We would like to clarify that **LTH is a three step process: 1) Train the dense network 2) Iterative pruning to find the sparse mask 3) Retrain the identified pruned mask in isolation to full accuracy.**
Most if not all existing well-established LTH literature use the same architecture blocks, initialization techniques, and training recipe used by dense networks in step 1.  However, it is not clear if blindly inheriting dense network protocols is optimal for sparse networks. We are first to raise a direct question on inheritance, and experimentally shown that making sparse re-training purposely misaligned in some way from dense training (step 3) can make the found sparse subnetwork work even better. We want to highlight that we are only making changes in the step 3 of LTH and completely independent of either dense training or identifying prune masks. This novelty has been also acknowledged by *Reviewer eSrF (‘inspiring challenger to many “commonsense” in LTH’)*

2) We are **first to identify a set of simple and well-defined techniques which can help sparse retraining step of LTH** to match the equivalent performance of the common practice of weight rewinding [1], which have many drawbacks (struggle to find rewind point, bookkeeping the weights of dense network during their training, entwine of rewind point to model architecture, etc) which has been appreciated by *Reviewer puN9 (‘compelling results for high sparsity as compared to LTH rewinding’)*. Even though these techniques have been known in the dense network training regime, they have been hidden/unexplored in sparse retraining step for LTH because of the clouded wisdom that sparse retraining need to stick to protocols of dense network training. *Reviewer eSrF acknowledges this as “established the improved sparse re-training step as a hidden gem”*.

**[Cons2: Experimental results are not solid since only image classification?]** The concern that we have only studied the task of image classification in our work, we would like to highlight that LTH has been primarily investigated for classification tasks in the literature (it’s common for nearly all SOTA papers); and its significance (lottery ticket retraining) for other tasks such as object detection/segmentation/keypoint estimation is still debated and have controversial results. For example - [2] argues that lottery tickets obtained from Imagenet pretraining do not transfer well to the downstream tasks of detection/segmentation. On the other hand, [3] has been able to locate lottery subnetworks at 59.04% to 96.48% sparsity that transfer universally to multiple downstream tasks, whose performance see no degradation compared to using full pre-trained weights. Hence, those tasks are not yet well-accepted benchmarks for LTH.  

In image classification, we would like to highlight that we have conducted *“thorough and strong”* (quoting **Reviewer eSrF**) experiments to show performance margins generalization across datasets (CIFAR10, CIFAR100, TinyImageNet) and architectures (Vgg16, ResNet-18/ResNet-34, MobileNet). 

[1] Frankle, Jonathan, et al. "Stabilizing the lottery ticket hypothesis." arXiv preprint arXiv:1903.01611 (2019).

[2] Girish, Sharath, et al. "The lottery ticket hypothesis for object recognition." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2021.

[3] Chen, Tianlong, et al. "The lottery tickets hypothesis for supervised and self-supervised pre-training in computer vision models." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2021.

display_title: Novelty and focus on image classification

content.title: Novelty and focus on image classification
content.comment:
Novelty of contribution: 
- I acknowledge that this combination of tweaks has not been explored in the context of the LTH hypothesis and that the tweaks can improve sparse training after the LT has been identified. However, the question remains whether this contribution is interesting and novel enough to meet the ICLR bar. My concerns are that the insights are not far reaching enough because (1) the tweaks are not new ideas in the context of deep learning and (2) the contribution of different factors is only analyzed superficially. Sometimes these tricks work, sometimes they don't. There is no additional LTH specific new intuition presented why or when they should work. 

- Contemplating about the story: Why would the authors focus their tweaks on sparse training after the LT has been identified? IMP specifically benefits from an iterative pruning - training (- resetting) procedure. Shouldn't the training during the IMP procedure also benefit from the tweaks? Shouldn't this also improve the overall LT pruning performance because IMP is more consistent with the training objective?
This line of thought actually questions that it makes sense to decouple the iterative pruning + training protocol from the later sparse training protocol, since the iterative pruning + training protocol is meant to optimize the later training of the LT. 
Did the authors check whether their tweaks during IMP can improve the whole approach further?

- Focus on image classification: I agree with the authors that most LT experiments focus on image classification benchmarks. For that reason I would also not request them to add different experiments. However, also other work in that field could benefit of broadening their horizon and consider different types of benchmarks.

content.title: Author Response to NPsy
content.comment:
**[Cons3: Significance of our tweaks and concern with smoothening]** We would like to clarify that each of our proposed tweaks play a significant and complementary role in improving the sparse retraining step of LTH (Fig 1) - some help significantly at low sparsity and some help at high sparsity. For example, our architecture tweaking techniques (skip connections and smooth neurons) tend to have high benefits for very high sparsity (which make sense considering the issue of high activation sparsity and layer collapse) while training recipe tweaks (layerwise scaling and label smoothening), we experimentally observe that they help at low sparsity possibly because of their smoothness capabilities, they help in generalization of overparameterized networks. The orthogonal benefit is very clearly stated in Fig 6 (a and b) and section 4.4, where when they are combined, they have similar (even better) performance than extremely costly weight rewinding process upto ~90% sparsity. **Reviewers sSrF and puN9** have both acknowledged the compelling performance improvement achieved by them. Moreover, Fig 1 illustrates that our tweaks have more impact on sparse retraining in comparison to when they are applied to dense counterparts and trained from the start. 

To make the improvements more clear, we summarize the improvement made by our tweaks in dense network and average improvement made by them in their sparse counterparts (average overall 16 levels of studied sparsity in Fig 1 - from 20% to 97%) in the following table [Resnet-18 + CIFAR100]. More detailed results are added in Appendix A1.3 of our revised version.

|Method|Skip Connection|Soft Activation-Swish|Soft Activation - Mish|Layerwise Scaling|Label Smoothening|
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
|Dense Network|-0.77|+0.21|+0.24|-0.05|+0.55|
|Sparse Network|+0.93|+0.73|+0.72|+0.43|+0.85|

The argument that if our tweaks can be viewed as smoothening has been experimentally verified in Figures 4, 9, and 11 along with appendix A1.2 and A1.7. We additionally provide evidence in Figure 2 with the help of eigenvalue analysis that sparse networks trained smooth neurons have significantly low top eigenvalues indicating the presence of high smoothness. To the best of our knowledge, we are first to explore the impact of smooth neurons in retraining lottery tickets identified by LTH. 

We provide an additional table for Hessian analysis (top eigenvalues of Hessian) of models trained with our tweaks (Resnet 18 + CIFAR100 + Epoch 180) below (using [1]) and we have included it in Appendix A1.7 of our revision. Note that these results mean over 10 random batches of test data.

|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|

[1] Yao, Zhewei, et al. "Pyhessian: Neural networks through the lens of the hessian." 2020 IEEE International Conference on Big Data (Big Data). IEEE, 2020.

**[Cons4: Concerns regarding comparison with pruning based methods]** We would like to clearly emphasize our tweaks have nothing to do with the specific pruning algorithm and can be easily plugged-in sparse masks identified by any other pruning technique (eg. [1],[2],[3]) and achieve performance benefits, although in our work we focus on pruned subnetworks identified by LTH. Note that we have followed exactly the best practice suggested in [4] for all networks and datasets in our experiments to identify LTH subnetworks for a fair comparison.

Following your suggestion, we have attempted to compare our technique results with other prevalent SOTA pruning methods and the results are summarized below (also included in Appendix A1.6). We will incorporate these in our final revised version. Moreover, appendix A1.4 illustrates the effectiveness of our tweaks when applied to *one-shot magnitude pruning*.

content.title: Are the tweaks problem specific or LT sparse training specific?
content.comment:
I thank the authors for adding experiments regarding the effect size of different tweaks, the smoothing, and one-shot pruning methods.

They do not really address my concerns though that the smoothing benefits etc. apply in general to the problem and are not specific to sparse training of the identified LT.

Note that synflow was also applied iteratively (not only initially without regarding data). Surely, the proposed tweaks can also be combined with other pruning techniques and it strengthens the paper to demonstrate this fact also in experiments.
I am insisting on comparisons with other methods simply to verify whether the authors achieve a new state of the art, which is a slightly different question. If the tweaks improve all considered LT methods, then, of course, the authors also achieve a new state of the art.

However, my main criticism remains that the tweaks might not be interesting enough on their own and that they might improve also IMP, which would not support the story that the authors distinguish their work from the rest by showing that decoupling sparse training of the LT should follow a different protocol than IMP.

content.title: Author Response to NPsy
content.comment:
We would like to thank you for concretely expressing your concern and we would like to provide additional experiments to address it. We added our tweaks into the dense training/IMP process (mask finding), and presented the results in the following table. Column 3 (AT-IMP + AT sparse training) indicates the performance of the mask identified when IMP is assisted with our architecture tweaks (soft-activation and skip-connection). Column 5 (TRT-IMP + TRT sparse training) indicates the performance of the mask identified when IMP is assisted with our training recipe tweaks (label smoothening and layer-wise initialization). It can be clearly observed that the performance significantly degrades (worse than vanilla-LTH) compared to using vanilla IMP and using our tweaks only at the sparse re-training step. 

We share our conjecture on these somewhat surprising observations: the dense architectures and training recipes have been so optimized for each network (somehow ``overfitting”), and tuning part of it usually cannot bring much benefits, and sometimes can hurt. For example, in the architecture tweaks (AT), it is well known that randomly adding more skip connections, without carefully optimizing their locations and configurations, won’t be helpful. That explains why AT integrated into dense training/IMP even hurts. For Training Recipe Tweaks (TRT), we observe label smoothening + re-initialization integrated into dense training/IMP indeed helps over the vanilla LTH, but was inferior to our Vanilla IMP + TRT sparse training.

Those results strengthen our argument: (1) while dense training/IMP is so optimized and hard to re-touch, it is non-optimal for sparse training to inherit them. Sparse training could explore its own training way, relatively independently of dense training/IMP. (2) while some of the proposed tweaks may improve dense training/IMP too, we found vanilla dense training/IMP + our tweaked sparse training to yield the best combination. That again supports the merits of adopting disentangled training ways for sparse networks. We believe no one has ever reported such an ablation study and hope the reviewer now is better convinced.

**[Cons5: Missing details for skip-connections and initialization]** - Many thanks for pointing out the missing details for our skip-connections and initialization techniques. We have added one skip-connection per layer as shown in Fig 3 to the pruned subnetworks identified from the LTH pruning step.  

We would like to clarify that the following questions are not in scope because we have nothing to do with the pruning step of LTH. We **FOCUS only on the sparse re-training** of the subnetworks identified after the LTH pruning/mask finding step.

1) Do the authors suggest that skip connections should only be added after aggressive pruning?
2) Are these skip connections actually pruned away or preserved? 
3) Is the layer thus effectively removed?
4) Do these parameter initializations respect different layer densities and different pruning stages?

Considering [2](pruning at initialization), which proposes rescaling tricks for training prune subnetworks, we would like to emphasize that their method has not explored pruned networks identified by LTH (post training pruning) and more importantly, their method is limited to FFNN and basic CNN blocks. They have clearly mentioned in their paper - *“An adaptation of the ReScaling trick to standard VGG architectures would be of great value and is left for future work.”* In our experiments, we have clearly shown that our rescaling method can be easily adapted not just for simple architectures like VGG, but also to more significantly used architectures such as ResNet-18/34 and MobileNet. Likewise [1], which develop a signal propagation perspective for pruning at initialization and used data-free method to recover the orthogonality and enhance trainability of the compressed network, has also not been studied in terms of LTH, and authors of the paper have clearly accepted that they are yet far from achieving subnetworks with equivalent capacity as identified by LTH - *“ We believe that our results on the increased trainability of compressed networks can take us one step towards finding winning lottery ticket by [4]”*. Tickets identified by LTH have very special property of being trained in isolation from scratch and Evci et al., 2020b have identified that we should not mess up very much with their default initialization. Our identified method is very cleverly making changes in their default initialization, which lead to performance improvement.

Finally, we would like to add that our tweaks are insensitive to hyperparameters and we have used exactly the same set of parameters for all our experiments across different datasets (CIFAR10, CIFAR100, TinyImageNet) and architectures (Vgg16, ResNet-18/ResNet-34, MobileNet). For layerwise rescaling we have used the best setting prescribed by GradInit [3] for SGD (ηmax = 0.15, and use η = 0.15, γ = 1) for all our experiments. For our label smoothening experiments, we have used smoothing factor alpha = 0.1

[Cons6: Visualization issue and Error Bars] Thanks for pointing this out. We will replace the figure in the revised version with axes details/error bars and add more explanations. We have plotted the loss functions in Fig 4, and 9 using filter-wise normalized directions proposed in [5] which handles several challenges such as scale invariance to make the geometry of loss surfaces from two different minimizers/networks compatible.

[1] A Signal Propagation Perspective for Pruning Neural Networks at Initialization, ICLR 2020. 

[2] Robust Pruning at Initialization, ICLR 2021. 

[3] Zhu, Chen, et al. "GradInit: Learning to initialize neural networks for stable and efficient training." arXiv preprint arXiv:2102.08098 (2021).

[4] Frankle, Jonathan, and Michael Carbin. "The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis: Finding Sparse, Trainable Neural Networks." International Conference on Learning Representations. 2018

[5] Li, Hao, et al. "Visualizing the Loss Landscape of Neural Nets." NIPS'18: Proceedings of the 32nd International Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems. Curran Associates Inc., 2018.


We hope our responses have clarified many of your concerns, and please do not hesitate to let us know what else we could do in order to convince you for a rating upgrade.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose that the training and structure of models found by lottery tickets rewinding (LTR)/lottery tickets (LT) should be modified from that of the dense model, unlike what was typically done in at least the original LT paper, and propose a set of training and architectural changes to improve retraining of these sparse models. The architectural changes consist of adding extra skip connections around each convolutional layer within the ResNet blocks, and changing the ReLU activation function to Swish/Mish. The training changes consist of scaling the LT initialization according to the sparsity of the layer and replacing the one-hot classification labels with naive or knowledge-distilled soft labels. The authors demonstrate improved generalization for the combination of all of these changes as compared to dense training and standard LTH retraining baselines with VGG16, ResNet-18/34 and MobileNet on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 and dense/standard LTH with (unclear what model) on Tiny-ImageNet. The authors claim significant generalization improvement for very sparse networks, e.g. +4.93% at 97% sparsity for ResNet-18/CIFAR-100.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
- Compelling results for high-sparsity as compared to LTH rewinding
- Figure 1(a) shows significantly higher improvement at high sparsity with the extra skip connections than at low sparsity/the baseline dense model. Using extra skip connections could be benefiting sparse NN more than dense from this result.
- Figure 6 shows significant improvements with MobileNet/CIFAR-100 in particular, but also to some extent ResNet 18/34 at high sparsity.
- Figure 2 presents some compelling results for the claim that the activation function changes from ReLU to Swish/Mish result in sparse NN that have smoother loss landscape - *however* this is already known for dense NN, as presented in Fig. 5 of the swish paper for example.

Weaknesses:
- While the authors motivate most of the changes in improving the smoothness of the loss landscape, there is little evidence (outside of the swish/mish activation functions) aside from some plots of the "loss surface"/"loss landscape" in Figure 5 and Figure 11 - but these visualizations are not explained at all, and clearly must be projections/transformations of the loss landscape. Without knowing how they were produced we can't judge how representative they are. Why not use the Hessian analysis as used for Swish/Mish to quantify this?
- Many of the proposed improvements seem to improve the performance of the baseline dense model and very-low sparsity models very significantly, making the question of if these results simply improve all DNN training rather than sparse/LTH training important. The authors attempt to address this question in Figure 1 by claiming the improvement increases for high sparsity, but it's not convincing for any of the results except for perhaps skip connections (Fig 1(a)), and in fact Fig 1(d) seems to show that label smoothing only helps the baseline dense or very low-sparsity models.
- There is no clear table of results, only graphs, making it hard to judge the actual significance of the results. The CIFAR10/100 experiments should have multiple runs with different seeds to judge the variance/significance of the presented differences which are marginal in much of Figure 1.
- There should also be a table of results presenting an ablation study over the many confounded methods (AT+TRT) used by the authors, like what the authors tried to show in Figure 1.
- Graphs often presented without proper labelling/explanatory captions. For example, what's the x axis in figure 8 and 6? Assuming sparsity, but should be clear.
- Graphs seem to be in an odd order, and far from where they are referenced, or are just not referenced in the text (Figure 8 for example).
- The initialization component of the method itself is not a contribution since as the authors cite, it was proposed elsewhere.
- Section 3.1: The motivation that having extra skip connections smooths the loss landscape is known, but why does this matter more for sparse NN than dense? The explanation that it might prevent collapsed layers (layers with catastrophic pruning) makes sense for (uncommon) extreme sparsity, but not so much for reasonably sparsity levels. 
- End of Section 3.2: The argument that scaling of the LTH initialization will not affect training because of batch norm is not valid, since batch norm takes a number of iterations to collect mini-batch statistics and will not be effective on the first number of iterations which can be very important for training. It is also a confusing argument since the authors learn coefficients to scale the LTH initialization to improve training as in Zhu et al., apparently acknowledging this.

Minor comments:
- Section 3: "However, those are not necessarily optimal for training sparse networks." Why? There is no justification or reference made for this statement here. If referring to the results, then state as our results demonstrate. 
- Section 3.1: claims "ReLU is an obstacle to sparse retraining because it leads to high activation sparsity in the subnetwork." No results are shown/cited here to back up this motivation, and it's not clear why activation sparsity should be more of a hindrance than with dense NN if the pruned connections were not salient. Should refer to appendix A1.
- Last line of 2.1 doesn't make sense, perhaps it means "in dense CNNs"?
content.summary_of_the_review: This is overall a poorly presented paper, with significant issues in the motivation and the presentation of results in particular, and is simply not of a standard of an ICLR paper in the current state. This is unfortunate as it does contain what could be some promising results, in particular for the architectural changes improving training at high sparsity. I would encourage the authors to work further on the presentation of the motivation and results, narrowing down the scope of their method to those changes with the most promising results vis-a-vis sparse NN, and incorporating the feedback for submission elsewhere, but I cannot recommend this paper for acceptance as is.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

Many thanks for reviewing our paper. We provide pointwise responses to your concerns.

**[Cons1: Missing evidence for smoothness and concerns with visualization plots]**
Thanks for pointing out that we can add additional Hessian analysis for all techniques to make our smoothening argument quantifiable. We are listing the table for Hessian results (Resnet 18 + CIFAR100 + Epoch 180) below and we will include them in our revision. Note that these results are mean over 10 random batches of test data. 

|Method||Sparsity Ratio||||
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
||20%|36%|67%||97%|
|Vanilla LTH|37.89|53.74|96.14||1098.74|
|LTH + Swish|34.25|39.42|63.03||334.92|
|LTH + Skip connection|31.11|53.12|90.08||985.78|
|LTH + Layerwise Rescale|32.66|50.84|94.83||1071.54|
|LTH + Label Smoothening|29.01|41.67|60.04||267.33

Our loss surface (Fig 4) and loss landscape (Fig 9) represents the smoothness impact of our tweaks during the early and final stages of our sparse networks in comparison with vanilla LTH (91% sparsity) identified from Resnet-18 on CIFAR100. We have plotted the loss functions using filter-wise normalized directions proposed in [1] which handles several challenges such as scale invariance to make geometry of loss surfaces from two different minimizers/networks compatible. It can be clearly observed from Fig 4 and 9 that our methods have played a significant role in making the loss plots smoother compared to vanilla LTH. Note that Fig 11 in ablation section 4.6 [comparison of loss landscape] studies the injected smoothness by making perturbations in the direction of top eigenvalues of Hessian matrix following [2]. Moreover, our appendix A1.2 also illustrates the convergence of our sparse retraining with tweaks to a much smoother minima with help of top eigenvalue analysis.

[1] Li, Hao, et al. "Visualizing the Loss Landscape of Neural Nets." NIPS'18: Proceedings of the 32nd International Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems. Curran Associates Inc., 2018.

[2] Yao, Zhewei, et al. "Pyhessian: Neural networks through the lens of the hessian." 2020 IEEE International Conference on Big Data (Big Data). IEEE, 2020.

**[Cons2: Not convincing improvements of our methods for various sparsity levels when compared to dense counterparts]** 
We would like to clarify that - 

(1) We did provide evidence to show our techniques boost sparse training in particular significantly, compared to dense training as shown in Fig 1. Our tweaks (skip-connections, and layerwise rescaling) actually decreased the dense network performance while our tweaks (soft-activation and label smoothening) performance gain is comparatively much higher in sparse networks compared to dense counterparts; 

(2) our proposed techniques have orthogonal improvements across different sparsity levels. For example, our architecture tweaking techniques (skip connections and smooth neurons) tend to have high benefits for very high sparsity (which make sense considering the issue of high activation sparsity and layer collapse) while training recipe tweaks (layerwise scaling and label smoothening), we experimentally observe that they help at low sparsity possibly because of their smoothness capabilities, they help in generalization of overparameterized networks. The orthogonal benefit is very clearly stated in Fig 6 (a and b) and section 4.4, where when they are combined, they have comparable (even better) performance than extremely costly weight rewinding process upto ~90% sparsity. Moreover, note that our identified tweaks make no changes to the critical and well-established step of iterative pruning for lottery ticket finding, so it can be easily plugged into any other pruning algorithm.

To make the improvements more clear, we summarize the improvement made by our tweaks in dense network and average improvement made by them in their sparse counterparts (average overall 16 levels of studied sparsity in Fig 1 - from 20% to 97%) in the following table [Resnet-18 + CIFAR100]. More detailed results are added in Appendix A1.3 of our revised version.

|Method|Skip Connection|Soft Activation-Swish|Soft Activation - Mish|Layerwise Scaling|Label Smoothening|
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
|Dense Network|-0.77|+0.21|+0.24|-0.05|+0.55|
|Sparse Network|+0.93|+0.73|+0.72|+0.43|+0.85|

**[Cons3: Missing error bars, no tables and only graphs, not organized graphs]** - Very thanks for pointing out the missing error bars for our Fig 1, some cosmetic issues, and we have added/resolved them in the revised draft. We are also thankful for your suggestion to include tables of results to provide better judgment and we have added it in our revised version (check appendix).

content.title: Cons1/Cons2 Reply
content.comment:
I'd like to thank the authors for their response to my review, and their efforts to clarify their method/results - I also apologize for my delayed reply. I will try and respond to each comment within the thread for ease of reading.

**[Cons1: Missing evidence for smoothness and concerns with visualization plots]** I assume the presented results are the eigenvalues of the Hessian as analyzed in [1]? As often in the paper itself, the context is not clearly explained above. If I am reading them correctly in that they show there is not a big difference in the smoothness of the loss landscape for LTH + Skip connection (and LTH + Layerwise Scaling), even at high sparsity. This is surprising for LTH + Skip in particular, and contrary to the results where Skip connections in particular see great success in improving very sparse training of LTH. I think this is a great improvement in quantitatively analyzing the smoothness of the loss landscape, but I'm not sure that these results support your results/and the hypothesis presented in the paper on why these measures are effective.

**[Cons2: Not convincing improvements of our methods for various sparsity levels when compared to dense counterparts]** 
This table is in the right direction - but it suffers all the same issues as the (original) Figure 1, not having the variance/test accuracies clearly in the table makes understanding the significance of the results difficult. Table A2 in the revised paper is much better, and approaching the ablation study I'd expect, although again missing the variances to make the significance of the differences in test accuracy apparent. 

I share concerns with Reviewer NPsy (and others) that, outside of perhaps skip connections and label smoothing in Figure 1, it's still not clear that these "tweaks" benefit sparse neural networks more than dense. I'm also confused as to why the results for all these plots at 20% are so different from the dense baselines, as I would expect the results to converge to the dense baselines as sparsity approaches zero. Unfortunately, despite putting a lot of work into producing more results and improving the paper's figures/tables, there doesn't seem to be an effort to address my concern that none of these "tweaks" is well motivated for sparse neural networks in particular outside of the vague argument about smoothing the loss landscape, which I don't believe even the new Hessian results concur with, and is not very sparse NN specific.

I do agree that there is a significant change in the test accuracy that is correlated with: (a) adding skip connections (increasing generalization for high sparsity) and (b) label (smoothing increasing generalization for low sparsity). However, just because these two "tweaks" show promise, and perhaps alone might make the basis for an interesting paper does not mean I can ignore the lack of significant evidence or motivation for the other "tweaks". As a reviewer (and a reader) of your paper we are forced to accept all of these disparate "tweaks" as a bundle at face value, and I feel that there simply is not enough evidence to accept the statement that all these "tweaks" together, ``boost sparse training in particular significantly, compared to dense training''. Furthermore there is little motivation as to why we should consider these tweaks bundled together as a method to begin with.

In general, bundling a bunch of tenuously related "tweaks" together in a paper with little motivation provides a much weaker benefit to the research community than instead diving deeper into experimenting, motivating and hopefully better understanding even one of these "tweaks" individually. For example, a paper demonstrating that skip connections disproportionately affect the generalization/trainability of sparse neural networks, together with a clear motivation and hypothesis as to why would be much better received.

**[Cons3: Missing error bars, no tables and only graphs, not organized graphs]**
The authors have made some improvements in this area which I thank them for, but the figures are still poorly explained in captions. Figure 1, for example, now has error bars, but there is nothing in the caption explaining what these error bars represent and we are referred to the appendix to find out.

content.title: Author response to puN9
content.comment:
**[Response related to Cons 1]** - We would like to clarify that our argument is - “our tweaks could be viewed as certain types of learned smoothening” and we have experimentally verified our argument with the help of Hessian analysis, loss landscapes, and loss counters (Fig 4,8 and Appendix A1.7). In each case, it can be clearly identified from our experiments that all of our tweaks have been able to reduce the top eigenvalues of Hessian, and smooth the loss landscape. HOWEVER, we would like to emphasize that we **never claimed that high smoothness means high performance gain or there exist any correlation between them**.  As pointed by you, there is not very high difference (~113 at 97% which actually is not very small and more than 1/10 of vanilla-LTH) in smoothness of LTH + Skip Connection, we would like to highlight that considering the complex dynamics of sparse optimization - it is not about introducing high amount of smoothness, but is about **INJECTING RIGHT AMOUNT OF SMOOTHNESS**.  It can be clearly inferred that even though label smoothening has been able to inject very high smoothness (80% of vanilla-LTH) in the sparse retraining at 97% sparsity, it doesn’t achieve enough performance benefit, which indicates that right proportion is important. These observations can open a new exploration door towards understanding the complex dynamics of sparse subnetwork optimization.

**[Missing motivation for using ‘tweaks’ and lack of novelty]**

We would like to **HIGHLIGHT** that our novelty is not using a bundle of tweaks, but it is challenging the conventional paradigm of LTH and validating that mis-aligning sparse retraining from the dense counterpart can be helpful to achieve better performance. More specifically, we identify the LTH sparse re-training goal and troubleshoot its overlooked problems (which is novel); and then refer to simple tools to solving those problems (we could have been “novel”, but we purposely avoid so since we believe no reinventing wheels is the right thing to do for science, if well-defined techniques can do the job right - “Simplicity is the final achievement. ”, well-said by Chopin). In other words, what makes this paper truly novel is knowing “where should be fixed”, besides (and more than) “how to concretely fix”.

Our paper’s novelty mainly lies in the following two aspects:

1. **Challenging prolonged LTH belief** that sparse ticket retraining should stick to the protocol of dense network training and sparse mask finding. We would like to clarify that **LTH is a three-step process: 1) Train the dense network 2) Iterative pruning to find the sparse mask 3) Retrain the identified pruned mask in isolation to full accuracy.** Most if not all existing well-established LTH literature use the same architecture blocks, initialization techniques, and training recipe used by dense networks in step 1. However, it is not clear if blindly inheriting dense network protocols is optimal for sparse networks. We are first to raise a direct question on inheritance, and experimentally shown that making sparse re-training purposely misaligned in some way from dense training (step 3) can make the found sparse subnetwork work even better. We want to highlight that we are only making changes in the step 3 of LTH and completely independent of either dense training or identifying prune masks. *This novelty has been also acknowledged by Reviewer eSrF (‘inspiring challenger to many “commonsense” in LTH’).*

2. Even though our techniques have been known in the dense network training regime, they have been hidden/unexplored in sparse retraining steps for LTH because of the clouded wisdom that sparse retraining needs to stick to protocols of dense network training. Reviewer eSrF acknowledges this as “established the improved sparse re-training step as a hidden gem”.

**[Minor errors on details in caption and plots]** We would be very thankful if you do not consider these cosmetic issues while making your decision. Even though the plots seem to be self-explanatory (along with error bars), we value your suggestion a lot and promise to fix it in the final version of our paper.

content.comment:
**[Clarification regarding the doubt -  confused as to why the results for all these plots at 20% are so different from the dense baselines, as I would expect the results to converge to the dense baselines as sparsity approaches zero.]** 

We would like to clarify that it is **not necessary that accuracy will have a very strict correlation with sparsity**. While it is common sense that with increase in spasticity, performance will suffer, but we would like to identify that tickets performances depend a lot on model architecture, dataset, and tickets itself (how well IMP has pruned). It is completely normal to observe tickets with 36% sparsity performing better than tickets with 20% sparsity and not necessarily convergence to dense when we approach zero (sparse networks have extremely complex training dynamics). If you will carefully look at our experiments in Figure 5, it can be observed that IMP tickets (ResNet-50 and CIFAR 100) at 20% sparsity performing better than its dense network while  IMP tickets (VGG 16 and CIFAR 10) at 20% sparsity have very close performance as dense network.

**[Response to concern related to Initialization]**  We would like to clarify that we didn’t claim that prior works have not tried re-init for sparse subnetworks. **Note that re-initializing a found sparse lottery ticket was unsuccessful before this paper**, as the initialization values of lottery tickets are believed to be particularly valuable and not to be perturbed - that differs from dense training where random (re)-initialization is much easier to work following some proper distribution (e.g., Kaiming initialization).  Both [PuN9-1] and [2], attempt to rescale the standard deviation of the gaussian distribution for the weight initialization. And they do re-init from random gaussian, in order to follow kaiming init and keep the gradient flow. While PuN9 has clearly mentioned - **“which however in our observations does not bring gains compared with unscaled counterparts”**, [4] experimentally validated that re-init can lead to catastrophic outcome of losing the lottery ticket drawn. They haven’t shown performance improvements with their re-init method. We would like to emphasize that, **we identified the hidden gem [3] and successfully demonstrated that it can work** and achieve performance benefits which can encourage researchers to rethink better initialization techniques for lottery tickets rather than relying on reusing dense initialization blindly.

**[Additional Benefits of our tweaks]** We would additionally like to emphasize again that **our tweaks have nothing to do with any specific pruning algorithm and can be easily plugged-in sparse masks identified by any other pruning technique** and achieve performance benefits. In this paper, we focus on the special pruning way of LTH, out of our team’s research focus. However, the proposed sparse training tweaks can apply together with any pruning algorithm too. To validate this, we show the performance benefit achieved by incorporating our tweaks in subnetworks identified by Random Pruning and SyncFlow as follows:

content.title: Author response to puN9
content.comment:
**[Cons4: Initialization method is not a contribution]** We agree that layerwise scaling was proposed by [3] but we want to highlight that it has been a hidden gem as pointed out by reviewer eSrF (strength 2) and it has never been identified that it can significantly help in the sparse retraining step of LTH. **Hence, we confidently claim our insights as a unique contribution for sparse LTH training, even after we explicitly acknowledged the existing proposal in [3].** Please see our rationale below.

Note that re-initializing a found sparse lottery ticket was unsuccessful before this paper, as the initialization values of lottery tickets are believed to be particularly valuable and not to be perturbed - that differs from dense training where random (re)-initialization is much easier to work following some proper distribution (e.g., Kaiming initialization). 

Most of the prior work in LTH uses the same initialization derived from their dense counterparts. [4] pointed out that blind usage of dense initialization will violate the Kaiming initialization (since the number of incoming and outgoing connections are not same) but meanwhile random reinitialization will lead to losing the lottery ticket drawn. As per our knowledge, none of the prior work formalized a better initialization strategy for the lottery tickets. 

Balancing between the concerns pointed by [4], we identified the hidden gem of layer-wise scaling of the weights of lottery tickets, which (1) doesn’t hurt the original LTH initialization geometry (it only scales the basic of attraction which can be absorbed by BN in feedforward); and meanwhile (2) is optimized towards loss descent. This is hence unique and novel, tightly tied to the aforementioned challenges of LTH.

Our experiments validate that this technique helps in injecting smoothness in the initial phase of training and help gain around +0.43% average improvement across all 16 levels of studied sparsity (20%-97%) - ref table in cons2.

[3] Zhu, Chen, et al. "GradInit: Learning to initialize neural networks for stable and efficient training." arXiv preprint arXiv:2102.08098 (2021).

[4] Utku Evci, Yani Andrew Ioannou, Cem Keskin, and Yann Dauphin. Gradient flow in sparse neural
networks and how lottery tickets win. ArXiv, abs/2010.03533, 2020b.

**[Cons5: Additional explanation for Skip connection performance]** As mentioned in section 3.1, skip connections on the sparse networks smoothen the landscape and preserve gradients, besides its possible mitigation effect when encountering collapsed layers. We agree with the comment that it matters more for extreme sparsity and it has been clearly reflected in our experimental results in Fig 1(a). Moreover, we would like to highlight that we have a bag of two orthogonal techniques that have different effects at different sparsity levels. One group(AT) had maximal improvements for high sparsity while the other(TRT) improved at low sparsity level. When combined and plugged in sparse training, they provide significant improvements for all sparsity levels. Depending on the problem at hand (what sparsity level), we can choose.

**[Cons6 : Argument Clarification - linear scaling will not hurt the original LTH initialization, thanks to the BatchNorm layer which will effectively absorb any linear scaling of the weights]** We would like to clarify your confusion that - “scaling of the LTH initialization will not affect training because of BN is not valid, since BN takes a number of iterations to collect mini-batch statistics and will not be effective on the first number of iterations which can be very important for training” by putting forward following arguments -

a) We have optimized a small set of scalar coefficients following[3] to make the first update step (e.g., using SGD) as effective as possible at lowering the training loss. After the scalar coefficients are learned, the original LTH initializations of subnetworks are re-scaled and the optimization proceeds as normal.

b) Yes, in the feedforward pass, BN absorbs any linear scaling so it is resilient to re-scaling - and this is what we exactly want - to preserve the good LTH basin. Please refer to Cons4 for more details. 

c)However, in the backward pass, the re-scaled init takes effect in modifying the gradients, which is not nullified by BN.

content.title: Cons4/Cons6 Reply
content.comment:
I'd like to thank the authors for their response to my review, and their efforts to clarify their method/results - I also apologize for my delayed reply. I will try and respond to each common within the thread for ease of reading.

**[Cons4: Initialization method is not a contribution]** From my understanding, your claim of novelty vis-a-vis scaled initialization as proposed in [3] is that you were the first to apply it in training a LT/sparse training, *however* this was a focus of [PuN9-1] (much earlier than [3,4]) where the authors focused on improving sparse training with a scaled-dense initialization in a layer-wise fashion, where the initialization is simply scaled by sparsity. This was also explored in [4], and compared with a "correct" sparsity aware initialization [4] proposed, showing that both were effective in improving sparse training in general. Your work shows that it may also improve training from LTs, a specific (albeit interesting) case of sparse training, but this is only marginally novel - and no comparison is made with the much simpler method proposed in [PuN9-1].

**[Cons6 : Argument Clarification]** 
In fact I don't disagree that scaling the initialization is helpful for training, but I think the whole point of this improved initialization is that training **is** affected by the better initialization in the first few steps, for the better, and these first few steps aren't helped by BN.

It's unclear to me how the backward pass (gradients) is claimed to be not affected by BN in the forward pass since the gradients are calculated w.r.t. the loss...  I might be misunderstanding the author's point here though?

content.summary_of_the_paper: In the lottery ticket hypothesis (LTH) literature, re-training a found lottery ticket is an often-underestimated step, just re-using the dense training protocols. This paper discovers the hidden gem of “tweaking” better sparse training and improves the lottery ticket quality even with the same found sparse mask.
content.main_review:
Pros. 
-  This paper is an inspiring challenger to many “commonsense” in LTH: once the sparse mask is obtained, traditionally, it has to be re-trained with the same initialization (or rewinding) and same training recipe as its dense network. This paper established the improved sparse re-training step as a hidden gem and showed the proposed tweaks could generalize to other sparse training methods in general. 
- Among the proposed tweaks, what impresses me most is the idea of changing the “lottery ticket initialization” by learned layer-wise scaling. While (Evci et al., 2020b) already pointed out typical dense initialization isn’t optimal for sparse NNs, they also found random re-initialization will destroy lottery tickets. This paper found a particularly clear idea between these two extremes by using learned linear scaling –– it can be learned to optimize the landscape for faster loss decrease while any linear coefficient can be absorbed by batch normalization. 
- Experiments are thorough and strong, showing improved sparse re-training clearly boosts the performance of “winning tickets” at high sparsity levels and large models. The performance margins are generalizable across datasets (CIFAR10, CIFAR100, TinyImageNet) and architectures (Vgg16, ResNet-18/ResNet-34, MobileNet). 
- The authors did a good job in connecting literature rationale with experimental observations, making their findings more comprehendible. I also liked the visualization in Figure 5 and Figure 11 and the ablation study results. Plus, due care has been made in distinguishing the techniques’ benefits to general (dense) training versus specifically sparse re-training. 

Cons.
- To be fair, many discoveries in this paper, although new to LTH, is not so “new” nor surprising in general deep learning literature, such as smoother neurons improving gradient flows (hence fixing sparse training, as Tessera et al., 2021 also found); as well as denser skipping connections, label smoothening, etc.
content.summary_of_the_review: The submission is a solid work supported by convincing experimental results. While some proposed techniques are not essentially very new, identifying the sparse re-training bottlenecks and connecting all these dots is a non-trivial contribution. The work further provides many useful reflections and understandings on what is essential in sparse training.

content.title: Author Response to Reviewer eSrF
content.comment:
Many thanks for identifying the significance of our work which questions common belief persisting in well-established LTH literature, i.e., sparse network retraining should stick to the protocol of dense network training and ticket finding process. We are very glad that you found our experiments strong, have coherence with the literature and appreciated the idea of playing with the initialization of lottery tickets. 

We agree with your view that many of our methods are known in deep learning literature, but new to LTH (specifically, as per our knowledge they have never been studied to improve the performance of lottery tickets in plug-n-play manner). We would like to highlight our observation about the orthogonal behavior of our tweaks where architecture tweaks (smooth neurons, skip-connections) play a significant role in improving tickets with high sparsity, while our training recipe tweaks (smoothening, initialization) helps at low sparsity. This provided us with an opportunity to combine them and achieve comparable (even better) performance than the extremely costly weight rewinding process up to ~90% sparsity. Moreover, our identified tweaks make no changes to the critical step of iterative pruning for lottery ticket finding, so it can be easily plugged into any other pruning algorithm. 

Note - We have added some additional interesting results in the Appendix section of our revised draft.
